**Eight practitioner assumptions and their negations**

1. Skip parents make downstream convs more valuable, since residual paths ease optimization. If false, an upstream skip leaves raw features that make a downstream conv redundant (#2), or it supplies a clean identity that the conv refines (#1, #19).
2. Pooling upstream loses information and caps downstream gains. If false, pooling smooths features and downstream convs recover more from them (#3, #5). If it holds, it is worse on low-resolution ImageNet16-120 (#4, #7).
3. Parallel routes into a node are redundant, so one conv lowers the value of another. If false, a sibling skip or conv makes the edited conv more valuable (#6, #9, #17, #18).
4. Stacking 3x3 convs grows the receptive field and so helps. If false, a 3x3 parent saturates the receptive field (#12), and a 1x1 parent leaves more room for a 3x3 child (#11).
5. Pruning hurts less when a bypass exists. If false, the bypass changes what pruning costs in a different way (#13, #14, #15).
6. The 0->3 shortcut makes other edges less important. If false, it makes deeper convs more valuable, because it covers the identity path (#6, #16).
7. A conv is always better than a skip. If false, a skip edit gains from a conv-heavy sibling route, because it adds gradient flow (#17, #19).
8. Interactions are consistent across datasets. This is the premise behind every hypothesis, since each must hold on all three datasets. The pooling hypotheses target ImageNet16-120 in particular.
